Kharazian said this dynamic means it has very much become a buyer’s market. Subsidizing use of expensive technology in order to lock in customers has always been a part of the Big Tech playbook. Just recall how cheap it used to be to take an Uber or Lyft ride, and now that there are few other ride-hail players, the cost of going from A to B has risen significantly. Notion co-founder Akshay Kothari recently posted internal data that matched Ramp’s insights. As he succinctly put it: “tokens go brrr. costs go ahhh.”
tokens go brrr costs go ahhh pic.twitter.com/1whCWCJCyM

“A lot of the assumptions that we had about the trajectory of AI spend are starting to break down,” Kharazian said. “You can use more AI, but use it for less. That’s great for the customers…but it’s not necessarily great for the model companies. And it does introduce new questions around their revenue trajectories.”

Bloomberg reported Friday that Anthropic’s potential valuation sank from the $2 trillion estimated in early October to just $1.2 to $1.3 trillion. The company is also reportedly expected to receive a high “junk” rating from credit agencies. OpenAI also lowered its proposed valuation to $1.25 trillion from $1.4 trillion and slashed its latest fundraising goals by about $10 billion.
Kharazian says Ramp’s dataset likely informs many investor concerns. There is, however, one potential brightside for spending trajectories, albeit a speculative one.

Much of the thesis for hypergrowth spending is that AI will undoubtedly introduce new use cases that will accelerate things. AI coding emerged just a year and a half ago as the most commercially viable product that has led Anthropic and OpenAI to becoming trillion-dollar companies. The hope among investors is that there will be another revolution that will drive further spend.

Some think personal agents will be the next coding agents. OpenAI , SpaceXAI , and Meta have all released their own personal agents, alongside startups like Instinct . Kharazian is skeptical, though, that personal agents, which are “not as economically productive as coding,” will provide the boost the industry needs for nonstop growth.

“The projection is that there will be new products being introduced that will drive further growth,” Kharazian said. “But based on what we can observe today and the products available and what is commercially advanced, AI spend has started to slow down.”

extraction.body: Black Doves, the sleek and sexy Netflix series about the complicated friendship between a spy played by Keira Knightley and an assassin played by Ben Whishaw, has returned for season 2. Here’s what we know about the odds that Black Doves will be renewed for season 3.The first season brought Knightley’s character Helen, a spy married to a prominent conservative politician, back into action in the aftermath of her lover’s murder. The second season shoves her into the spotlight as her husband becomes prime minister. As various secret organizations and powers that be pull their strings to use them as pawns, the two of them can really only trust each other.Has Black Doves officially been renewed for season 3?As of the season 2 release, Black Doves has not yet been renewed for season 3. The second season was announced before the first season dropped on Netflix. But maybe the show was initially “ordered” for two seasons, and they announced it as an early renewal to create some well-deserved buzz before the premiere.So far, season 2 reviews have been good. If the audiences follow, then we should (hopefully) get the good news soon.What could Black Doves season 3 be about?No spoilers, but season 2 leaves a lot up in the air. I wouldn’t be surprised if a third season went international again. Every story about a spy and/or assassin teaches us that you can’t escape your past.However, since Black Doves is not based on a preexisting book series or film, it is difficult to decipher what happens next. That’s up to creator Joe Barton, who of course also created The Lazarus Project and recently adapted the play Amadeus to the small screen.When would Black Doves season 3 premiere on Netflix?This is the thing. There were two years between Black Doves season 1 and season 2. Scheduling can be difficult.But are we really going to have to wait until 2028 for Black Doves season 3? With all of the twists and turns of a show like this, you’ll need to do a total preseason series rewatch to remember what happened. If it is 2028, it’ll probably drop in November or December.

Eleanor and Williams have taken out paid hits on Laila and Sam, while Sam's final target in his prison-break contract with Kestrel is none other than Reed (after episode 4 revealed that she is in fact the mysterious “Wildflower” of the files she tried to take from Alexi Chernov).The main action kicks off when the precious international peace summit that Wallace (Andrew Buchan) has spent the whole season planning gets upended before it even starts. Wallace and Helen's cab is intercepted and chased, while U. S. defense envoy Cecile Mason (Neve Campbell) and recently widowed Russian envoy Katia Chernov (Sylvia Hoeks) are captured by strange armed men.When Patrick (Sam Riley), the Kestrel man who's been blackmailing Sam all season, escorts Reed back into the Black Doves office with a gun to her head, it quickly becomes clear that 'Wildflower', or Reed, is the only target Kestrel wants brought in alive. But she doesn't last long after a game of grenade hot potato played by Eleanor, Williams, and Laila ends with Dani being caught in a lift with it. Reed (Sarah Lancashire), is ensnared in a ruthless plot to undermine her position in the Black Doves, Helen is reunited with her best friend, Sam (Ben Whishaw).

extraction.body: Black Doves, the sleek and sexy Netflix series about the complicated friendship between a spy played by Keira Knightley and an assassin played by Ben Whishaw, has returned for season 2. Here’s what we know about the odds that Black Doves will be renewed for season 3.The first season brought Knightley’s character Helen, a spy married to a prominent conservative politician, back into action in the aftermath of her lover’s murder. The second season shoves her into the spotlight as her husband becomes prime minister. As various secret organizations and powers that be pull their strings to use them as pawns, the two of them can really only trust each other.Has Black Doves officially been renewed for season 3?As of the season 2 release, Black Doves has not yet been renewed for season 3. The second season was announced before the first season dropped on Netflix. But maybe the show was initially “ordered” for two seasons, and they announced it as an early renewal to create some well-deserved buzz before the premiere.So far, season 2 reviews have been good. If the audiences follow, then we should (hopefully) get the good news soon.What could Black Doves season 3 be about?No spoilers, but season 2 leaves a lot up in the air. I wouldn’t be surprised if a third season went international again. Every story about a spy and/or assassin teaches us that you can’t escape your past.However, since Black Doves is not based on a preexisting book series or film, it is difficult to decipher what happens next. That’s up to creator Joe Barton, who of course also created The Lazarus Project and recently adapted the play Amadeus to the small screen.When would Black Doves season 3 premiere on Netflix?This is the thing. There were two years between Black Doves season 1 and season 2. Scheduling can be difficult.But are we really going to have to wait until 2028 for Black Doves season 3? With all of the twists and turns of a show like this, you’ll need to do a total preseason series rewatch to remember what happened. If it is 2028, it’ll probably drop in November or December.

But this time around, Black Doves spends some time unravelling her past, as well as that of the titular intelligence agency: a backstory that informs and explains the major threat of the season, the German anarchist organization Kestrel.Though the secrets reveal themselves slowly, a bombshell-filled (pun very much intended) finale crashes through a series of twists that—if you didn't see them coming (which I can't say I did, for some of them)—will really feel like a stab in the face.

S. defense envoy Cecile Mason (Neve Campbell) and recently widowed Russian envoy Katia Chernov (Sylvia Hoeks) are captured by strange armed men.When Patrick (Sam Riley), the Kestrel man who's been blackmailing Sam all season, escorts Reed back into the Black Doves office with a gun to her head, it quickly becomes clear that 'Wildflower', or Reed, is the only target Kestrel wants brought in alive.

He leaves Helen with his card, more as a threat than anything else.Reed and Helen agree to increase Helen's standing and role within the Black Doves, meaning that she'll be more than just an intel-grabber going forward, and putting her in a pretty good spot work-wise.

extraction.body: After a two-year wait, Netflix's Christmas crime caper Black Doves is finally back for its second outing. It's a messy delight that tests the loyalties of the central characters in ways the first season never dared and—both annoyingly and excitingly—ends on just as agonizing a cliffhanger.In the first season, Elizabeth Reed (Sarah Lancashire) was something of a mystery: an ominous, witty controller of sorts who kept Helen Webb (Keira Knightley) and Sam Young (Ben Whishaw) on their toes. But this time around, Black Doves spends some time unravelling her past, as well as that of the titular intelligence agency: a backstory that informs and explains the major threat of the season, the German anarchist organization Kestrel.Though the secrets reveal themselves slowly, a bombshell-filled (pun very much intended) finale crashes through a series of twists that—if you didn't see them coming (which I can't say I did, for some of them)—will really feel like a stab in the face. No, not the back, because unfortunately the answers were always lying right in front of us.There's a lot to break down from that last episode, so read on for our recap of Black Doves season 2 and an explanation of the ending—including that twist that'll probably have a drastic impact on where we'll be at the beginning of season 3.Breaking Down Black Doves Season 2, Episode 6The penultimate episode ended with a bunch of crossed wires, conflicting contracts, and potential deaths. Eleanor and Williams have taken out paid hits on Laila and Sam, while Sam's final target in his prison-break contract with Kestrel is none other than Reed (after episode 4 revealed that she is in fact the mysterious “Wildflower” of the files she tried to take from Alexi Chernov).The main action kicks off when the precious international peace summit that Wallace (Andrew Buchan) has spent the whole season planning gets upended before it even starts. Wallace and Helen's cab is intercepted and chased, while U. S. defense envoy Cecile Mason (Neve Campbell) and recently widowed Russian envoy Katia Chernov (Sylvia Hoeks) are captured by strange armed men.When Patrick (Sam Riley), the Kestrel man who's been blackmailing Sam all season, escorts Reed back into the Black Doves office with a gun to her head, it quickly becomes clear that 'Wildflower', or Reed, is the only target Kestrel wants brought in alive. Or, at least, whoever's running it does.And there's the twist: after a horrid little hostage situation in the office results in the deaths of quite a few senior Black Doves and Mason, Katia reveals that she is in fact the head of Kestrel and, in turn, Vita—the long-lost, abandoned daughter that Reed left in Berlin after killing her fake husband and running off (ouch).Dani, the nuisance of a secretary Reed planted in Wallace's office to seduce him and potentially replace Helen, has ended up being recruited by Kestrel. But she doesn't last long after a game of grenade hot potato played by Eleanor, Williams, and Laila ends with Dani being caught in a lift with it. Even Reed's capable of mistakes.What Happens to Helen Webb?Meanwhile, over in the car park where Helen and Wallace end up after fleeing, Mr. Prime Minister finally decides to question his wife about her past and her secrets. Obviously, she lies again—until the situation shifts a little.Helen receives a series of ominous messages and threatening instructions, first over text, then through a discreet earpiece planted in her car. Katia, whom Helen very quickly realizes is not an ally, instructs her to kill Wallace and turn herself in to MI5. But what's the leverage, you ask?Marie, the housekeeper who was teased as a Black Dove at the end of the first season, has in fact been working for Kestrel this whole time. If you're a babysitter to the Prime Minister's spy wife, who's been planted by a capitalist intelligence agency, but you're working for a German anarchist organization, does that make you a double or a triple agent? A nightmare for Mrs Webb, more than anything.Helen tricks Katia over the phone by shooting past Wallace towards the window, explains (on a surface level) that the children are in danger and she needs to hijack the car, and darts off with Sam to rescue the children from Marie.After confronting Marie, Helen shoots her in the head and flees the scene, while Reed reconciles (not quite) with her bleeding-out daughter in her last moments. Obviously not, because it's never that simple.What’s Next for the Characters?MI5 is even more suspicious of Helen than ever before, but Wallace is covering for her. Conteh, as one of the few surviving senior members of the Black Doves, restores Reed to her former standing.Helen and Sam reconcile properly after their heated argument during the first Reed rescue mission of the season, and he reveals that he's going to leave the country once again. After they part, a strange man bumps into Helen and, BOOM, final twist! Patrick has escaped in perfect condition and Kestrel is still going strong. He leaves Helen with his card, more as a threat than anything else.Reed and Helen agree to increase Helen's standing and role within the Black Doves, meaning that she'll be more than just an intel-grabber going forward, and putting her in a pretty good spot work-wise. However, things aren't quite so simple at home.Wallace confronts Helen once again about her real name (Lily Morris), and the finale ends with what appears to be the beginning of a conversation about her past. But how much is Helen actually going to tell Wallace?

relevantPassages.text: No, not the back, because unfortunately the answers were always lying right in front of us.There's a lot to break down from that last episode, so read on for our recap of Black Doves season 2 and an explanation of the ending—including that twist that'll probably have a drastic impact on where we'll be at the beginning of season 3.Breaking Down Black Doves Season 2, Episode 6The penultimate episode ended with a bunch of crossed wires, conflicting contracts, and potential deaths.

But this time around, Black Doves spends some time unravelling her past, as well as that of the titular intelligence agency: a backstory that informs and explains the major threat of the season, the German anarchist organization Kestrel.Though the secrets reveal themselves slowly, a bombshell-filled (pun very much intended) finale crashes through a series of twists that—if you didn't see them coming (which I can't say I did, for some of them)—will really feel like a stab in the face.

S. defense envoy Cecile Mason (Neve Campbell) and recently widowed Russian envoy Katia Chernov (Sylvia Hoeks) are captured by strange armed men.When Patrick (Sam Riley), the Kestrel man who's been blackmailing Sam all season, escorts Reed back into the Black Doves office with a gun to her head, it quickly becomes clear that 'Wildflower', or Reed, is the only target Kestrel wants brought in alive.

He leaves Helen with his card, more as a threat than anything else.Reed and Helen agree to increase Helen's standing and role within the Black Doves, meaning that she'll be more than just an intel-grabber going forward, and putting her in a pretty good spot work-wise.
After a two-year wait, Netflix's Christmas crime caper Black Doves is finally back for its second outing.

It's a messy delight that tests the loyalties of the central characters in ways the first season never dared and—both annoyingly and excitingly—ends on just as agonizing a cliffhanger.In the first season, Elizabeth Reed (Sarah Lancashire) was something of a mystery: an ominous, witty controller of sorts who kept Helen Webb (Keira Knightley) and Sam Young (Ben Whishaw) on their toes.

extraction.body: Investing.com -- OpenAI will continue to invest in artificial intelligence infrastructure despite voter opposition to data centers in Tuesday's midterm elections, CFO Sarah Friar said Friday. Still guessing which stocks will beat the market? Our AI portfolio updates monthly and is outperforming the S&P 500 by 118%. See this month's list » "When I think about the midterms, I need to keep thinking about how do we keep investing to meet that customer demand," Friar told CNBC's Sara Eisen at the Citi TMT Leadership Summit in Pebble Beach, California. "It starts early with having built relationships with all of the hyperscalers, and it will continue to mean that we raise capital." Voters rejected data center development across the country on Tuesday. Out of 41 local ballot measures across 10 states, voters backed restrictions or rejected pro-development measures in all but one, according to an analysis by Ballotpedia and additional results gathered by CNBC on Wednesday. Americans grew worried about potential environmental harm, higher utility bills and job loss. The Nasdaq on Thursday posted its steepest drop in 19 months, led by declines in chipmaker and neocloud company shares tied to AI buildout. The stocks recovered partially on Friday. Unsure what to buy ahead of earnings? Our AI's recent pre-earnings calls delivered gains of +77% to +118% after results dropped. See this month's earnings picks » Friar said the election results did not dramatically change anything for OpenAI. The company published a policy blueprint and commitments on Thursday that it pledged to apply to company-owned and operated data centers in the future. "If the midterm means more focus on data centers and communities, we're going to keep doing the work to get into those communities and to build trust with them," Friar said. OpenAI filed its prospectus confidentially with the Securities and Exchange Commission in June. Friar said Friday the company would continue to look into a 2027 debut. Anthropic, OpenAI's main rival, aims to list on the Nasdaq in mid-November. Anthropic's revenue in the first nine months of the year rose roughly 1,200% to $33.2 billion, according to its prospectus. The company entered into purchase commitments and lease agreements with an aggregate committed spend of about $895.4 billion, substantially all related to compute and infrastructure. OpenAI is in talks to raise funding at a $1.25 billion pre-money valuation, Friar said Friday. She said "a good CFO always raises money when she can" and that the round is ongoing. "The demand for AI is real," Friar said. "I don't think anyone's arguing with that, or if they are, I think it's a losing argument." sources.title: After the midterms, things are looking rocky for Elon Musk and data centers
passages: On the latest episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast , Kirsten Korosec, Sean O’Kane, and I discussed what the midterms mean for the tech industry.

Sean kicked it off by noting that Elon Musk “seems to have basically nothing out of donating half a billion dollars” to Republicans, while his companies are now headquartered “in a state that has, remarkably, turned about as blue as it could possibly turn.”

Anthony: One thing I want to emphasize is that they’re calling it this [their] “compute campus policy.” And part of what that’s doing, beyond laying out these policy changes, is also an attempt to rebrand data centers, because they have become such a toxic phrase.

Because in the spirit of making threatening things seem cute, they should 100% create a compute campuses avatar, [a] cutesy thing, and then just present that instead of a power-, energy-sucking, water-sucking data center.

extraction.body: Democrats’ historic victory in this week’s midterm elections could also have a dramatic effect on the tech industry. In dozens of local ballot measures, voters rejected data centers . And even when they weren’t voting on the issue directly, they were electing politicians — like Texas’ new governor-elect Gina Hinojosa — who campaigned on the promise of restricting data centers. On the latest episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast , Kirsten Korosec, Sean O’Kane, and I discussed what the midterms mean for the tech industry. Sean kicked it off by noting that Elon Musk “seems to have basically nothing out of donating half a billion dollars” to Republicans, while his companies are now headquartered “in a state that has, remarkably, turned about as blue as it could possibly turn.” And Kirsten said that while data centers probably weren’t the main cause of the “blue wave,” they’ve become an “an increasingly grassroots issue, in part because of how hyperscalers and companies have gone about” getting their projects approved. And now, “we’re already seeing companies like OpenAI all of a sudden go, ‘Actually, we can change our policies.’” Keep reading for a preview of our conversation , edited for length and clarity. Sean O’Kane: First off, let’s talk about the fact that one of the biggest data center builders was also the largest donor to the Republican Party. Elon Musk seems to have gotten basically nothing out of donating half a billion dollars — maybe even more, by the time we see the final count — and in fact is now sitting there with all of his businesses in a state that has, remarkably, turned about as blue as it could possibly turn for the first time in a very long time, if ever. That, I think, is the biggest thing hanging above a lot of this discussion. But, there were also a bunch of ballot measures up around the country that would have paved the way for data centers to get built faster. Almost all of them got shot down, or voted against. [Actually, many of the ballot measures would have imposed restrictions or moratoriums on data centers, and almost all of those measures passed.] With [Democrats] in power, there is a consensus view, at least in the tech world, that this is going to mean we have a lot of roadblocks ahead for data centers, especially in places like Texas, where [you have] folks like the governor-elect [Gina] Hinojosa, who has spoken pretty openly about this being a campaign promise and something that she wants to focus on once she takes power, now that she’s beaten Greg Abbott. It’s the thing that I think the tech world is maybe a little too focused on. I’m curious what you guys think about that. Anthony Ha: I don’t necessarily think that they’re too focused on it, but I understand why it would feel a little bit disproportionate — the data center ballot measures, certainly there were a number of them, but it wasn’t something that was on the ballot everywhere. And in different races, the dynamic might have been a bit different, but there was this undercurrent and sense that it seems to be an issue that reaches across the country, that is bipartisan in a lot of ways, but that the Democrats seem to have been more effective at harnessing that energy. And of course, there’s all kinds of reasons why the Democrats did so well on Tuesday, but it does seem like anti-AI and especially anti-data center sentiment was a big part of it. That seems like a pretty potent political force. The next two years, [and] potentially beyond that, are going to be more difficult for tech companies in general, and hyperscalers, data center companies in particular. I also imagine that they have to be a little bit worried about: Is this going to continue to be an issue, not just with the people who got elected this year, but potentially in 2028 and beyond? Kirsten Korosec: Absolutely. I don’t think that the data center issue is what brought everyone to the polls and led to the quote-unquote “blue wave.” However, I will say that data centers have been an increasingly grassroots issue, in part because of how hyperscalers and companies have gone about getting these data centers [approved] — very secretive, oftentimes requiring NDAs of a elected officials or appointed officials, not sharing information about the scale of a project in very environmentally sensitive areas, including in the Southwest, where there’s very much a water scarcity issue. So I think that a lot of folks — Republicans, independents, and Democrats — all saw this as wrong. They were motivated by it, but I don’t think it was a singular issue. Now, here’s the interesting thing. There was a lot of waving of hands about how [AI companies] can’t possibly operate under any other circumstances. And we’re already seeing companies like OpenAI all of a sudden go, “Actually, we can change our policies.” They just released what they call a compute campus policy blueprint . And guess what? They’re not going to require NDAs anymore. They’re going to share their plans and supposedly operate in less secrecy. I think what this shows is that when you put up either a regulatory certainty in the marketplace, or at least signals of going in that direction, then corporations will respond. If you don’t do that, they will not necessarily do the thing that we hope that they will do. Anthony: One thing I want to emphasize is that they’re calling it this [their] “compute campus policy.” And part of what that’s doing, beyond laying out these policy changes, is also an attempt to rebrand data centers, because they have become such a toxic phrase. So they’re not data centers anymore, they are compute campuses, and I’m curious, whether either of you think that’ll take. Sean: I mean, this is ridiculous. Come on. It’s not going to change anything. It’s going to cause them more effort. For a company that likes to say that it’s no longer focused on side quests, OpenAI still loves to go in different directions a lot. And this is just the latest kind of thing where it’s just like: Why are you spending time on this at all? It doesn’t really seem like it’s going to move the needle. Kirsten: I have a great idea for OpenAI. Because in the spirit of making threatening things seem cute, they should 100% create a compute campuses avatar, [a] cutesy thing, and then just present that instead of a power-, energy-sucking, water-sucking data center. Anthony: And if these are just lovely compute campuses, they should just build their own offices there or work next door, see how that works out for them. Something else that I’m wondering about is, to what extent the election is maybe the second part of a one-two punch. [We’ve just seen] a big shift in how Wall Street is reacting to a lot of these hyperscalers and AI companies and this sense that [investors] are not excited about the idea that they should be spending all this money building new data centers, spending all this money on compute. And so there’s a financial incentive not to build all these data centers. I’m very curious how that’s going to play out. [From a regulatory standpoint,] it’s probably going to be harder to build data centers. Wall Street is probably not going to reward you for building data centers. But at the same time, to get to the scale that they want to get to, they are probably going to need to build data centers somewhere. Still guessing which stocks will beat the market? Our AI portfolio updates monthly and is outperforming the S&P 500 by 118%. See this month's list » "When I think about the midterms, I need to keep thinking about how do we keep investing to meet that customer demand," Friar told CNBC's Sara Eisen at the Citi TMT Leadership Summit in Pebble Beach, California. "It starts early with having built relationships with all of the hyperscalers, and it will continue to mean that we raise capital." Voters rejected data center development across the country on Tuesday. Out of 41 local ballot measures across 10 states, voters backed restrictions or rejected pro-development measures in all but one, according to an analysis by Ballotpedia and additional results gathered by CNBC on Wednesday. Americans grew worried about potential environmental harm, higher utility bills and job loss. The Nasdaq on Thursday posted its steepest drop in 19 months, led by declines in chipmaker and neocloud company shares tied to AI buildout. The stocks recovered partially on Friday. "If the midterm means more focus on data centers and communities, we're going to keep doing the work to get into those communities and to build trust with them," Friar said. OpenAI filed its prospectus confidentially with the Securities and Exchange Commission in June. Friar said Friday the company would continue to look into a 2027 debut. Anthropic, OpenAI's main rival, aims to list on the Nasdaq in mid-November. Anthropic's revenue in the first nine months of the year rose roughly 1,200% to $33.2 billion, according to its prospectus. The company entered into purchase commitments and lease agreements with an aggregate committed spend of about $895.4 billion, substantially all related to compute and infrastructure. OpenAI is in talks to raise funding at a $1.25 billion pre-money valuation, Friar said Friday. She said "a good CFO always raises money when she can" and that the round is ongoing. "The demand for AI is real," Friar said. "I don't think anyone's arguing with that, or if they are, I think it's a losing argument." extraction.body: Democrats’ historic victory in this week’s midterm elections could also have a dramatic effect on the tech industry. In dozens of local ballot measures, voters rejected data centers . And even when they weren’t voting on the issue directly, they were electing politicians — like Texas’ new governor-elect Gina Hinojosa — who campaigned on the promise of restricting data centers. On the latest episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast , Kirsten Korosec, Sean O’Kane, and I discussed what the midterms mean for the tech industry. Sean kicked it off by noting that Elon Musk “seems to have basically nothing out of donating half a billion dollars” to Republicans, while his companies are now headquartered “in a state that has, remarkably, turned about as blue as it could possibly turn.” And Kirsten said that while data centers probably weren’t the main cause of the “blue wave,” they’ve become an “an increasingly grassroots issue, in part because of how hyperscalers and companies have gone about” getting their projects approved. And now, “we’re already seeing companies like OpenAI all of a sudden go, ‘Actually, we can change our policies.’” Keep reading for a preview of our conversation , edited for length and clarity. Sean O’Kane: First off, let’s talk about the fact that one of the biggest data center builders was also the largest donor to the Republican Party. Elon Musk seems to have gotten basically nothing out of donating half a billion dollars — maybe even more, by the time we see the final count — and in fact is now sitting there with all of his businesses in a state that has, remarkably, turned about as blue as it could possibly turn for the first time in a very long time, if ever. That, I think, is the biggest thing hanging above a lot of this discussion. But, there were also a bunch of ballot measures up around the country that would have paved the way for data centers to get built faster. Almost all of them got shot down, or voted against. [Actually, many of the ballot measures would have imposed restrictions or moratoriums on data centers, and almost all of those measures passed.] With [Democrats] in power, there is a consensus view, at least in the tech world, that this is going to mean we have a lot of roadblocks ahead for data centers, especially in places like Texas, where [you have] folks like the governor-elect [Gina] Hinojosa, who has spoken pretty openly about this being a campaign promise and something that she wants to focus on once she takes power, now that she’s beaten Greg Abbott. It’s the thing that I think the tech world is maybe a little too focused on. I’m curious what you guys think about that. Anthony Ha: I don’t necessarily think that they’re too focused on it, but I understand why it would feel a little bit disproportionate — the data center ballot measures, certainly there were a number of them, but it wasn’t something that was on the ballot everywhere. And in different races, the dynamic might have been a bit different, but there was this undercurrent and sense that it seems to be an issue that reaches across the country, that is bipartisan in a lot of ways, but that the Democrats seem to have been more effective at harnessing that energy. And of course, there’s all kinds of reasons why the Democrats did so well on Tuesday, but it does seem like anti-AI and especially anti-data center sentiment was a big part of it. That seems like a pretty potent political force. The next two years, [and] potentially beyond that, are going to be more difficult for tech companies in general, and hyperscalers, data center companies in particular. I also imagine that they have to be a little bit worried about: Is this going to continue to be an issue, not just with the people who got elected this year, but potentially in 2028 and beyond? Kirsten Korosec: Absolutely. I don’t think that the data center issue is what brought everyone to the polls and led to the quote-unquote “blue wave.” However, I will say that data centers have been an increasingly grassroots issue, in part because of how hyperscalers and companies have gone about getting these data centers [approved] — very secretive, oftentimes requiring NDAs of a elected officials or appointed officials, not sharing information about the scale of a project in very environmentally sensitive areas, including in the Southwest, where there’s very much a water scarcity issue. So I think that a lot of folks — Republicans, independents, and Democrats — all saw this as wrong. They were motivated by it, but I don’t think it was a singular issue. Now, here’s the interesting thing. There was a lot of waving of hands about how [AI companies] can’t possibly operate under any other circumstances. And we’re already seeing companies like OpenAI all of a sudden go, “Actually, we can change our policies.” They just released what they call a compute campus policy blueprint . And guess what? They’re not going to require NDAs anymore. They’re going to share their plans and supposedly operate in less secrecy. I think what this shows is that when you put up either a regulatory certainty in the marketplace, or at least signals of going in that direction, then corporations will respond. If you don’t do that, they will not necessarily do the thing that we hope that they will do. Anthony: One thing I want to emphasize is that they’re calling it this [their] “compute campus policy.” And part of what that’s doing, beyond laying out these policy changes, is also an attempt to rebrand data centers, because they have become such a toxic phrase. So they’re not data centers anymore, they are compute campuses, and I’m curious, whether either of you think that’ll take. Sean: I mean, this is ridiculous. Come on. It’s not going to change anything. It’s going to cause them more effort. For a company that likes to say that it’s no longer focused on side quests, OpenAI still loves to go in different directions a lot. And this is just the latest kind of thing where it’s just like: Why are you spending time on this at all? It doesn’t really seem like it’s going to move the needle. Kirsten: I have a great idea for OpenAI. Because in the spirit of making threatening things seem cute, they should 100% create a compute campuses avatar, [a] cutesy thing, and then just present that instead of a power-, energy-sucking, water-sucking data center. Anthony: And if these are just lovely compute campuses, they should just build their own offices there or work next door, see how that works out for them. Something else that I’m wondering about is, to what extent the election is maybe the second part of a one-two punch. [We’ve just seen] a big shift in how Wall Street is reacting to a lot of these hyperscalers and AI companies and this sense that [investors] are not excited about the idea that they should be spending all this money building new data centers, spending all this money on compute. And so there’s a financial incentive not to build all these data centers. I’m very curious how that’s going to play out. [From a regulatory standpoint,] it’s probably going to be harder to build data centers. Wall Street is probably not going to reward you for building data centers. But at the same time, to get to the scale that they want to get to, they are probably going to need to build data centers somewhere. extraction.body: Democrats' historic victories in this week's U.S. midterm elections could also transform the tech industry. The public voted on 41 data center-related ballot measures on Tuesday — in all but one, the majority voted to impose more restrictions on data center development. And even when data centers weren't on the ballot directly, they were a major talking point, with newly-elected Democratic governors and congressmembers likely to support additional regulation . On the latest episode of TechCrunch's Equity podcast, Kirsten Korosec, Sean O'Kane, and Anthony Ha discuss what the election will mean for the tech industry moving forward — not just when it comes to data centers (which OpenAI is already trying to rebrand ), but also increased government scrutiny of Big Tech.

The company's existing relationships with many corporations that continue to rely on its GPUs can enable it to offer these clients other hardware and services that complement -- and work best with -- its GPUs for training, deploying, and running AI models. Its cloud business is booming, in part thanks to its library of AI services. It has also integrated AI across its productivity suite. passages: Bitcoin has traded below its global price on Coinbase for 61 days, but the tiny 0.13% gap may understate quiet over-the-counter buying by U.S. investors.
This information comes from a post by Coinbase Markets on X, published on November 6, 2026.
The gap, known as the Coinbase premium, is at -0.13%, placing it in the bottom 8% of readings from the past two years.
We believe the 61-day discount on Coinbase reflects this hesitation rather than a complete retreat from Bitcoin.
When these U.S. buyers outbid overseas traders, Coinbase tends to trade at a premium.
Conversely, when they pull back, a discount emerges.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
Coinbase pays us for certain activity generated through this link.
ETF outflows, the Coinbase discount, and Bitcoin's correlation with stocks all point to the same American investor.
The streak's length depends on who is measuring it.
This premium figure also has a crucial limitation.
As a result, the discount could look the same even if American investors are quietly accumulating Bitcoin off-exchange.
Even so, the discount alone doesn't mark a floor, since the premium has turned positive only after Bitcoin rebounded.
The second is a daily close above the 20-day average of $79,641, then above the 50-day average of $81,974, near where recent buyers break even.
When stock investors reduce their risk, they often sell Bitcoin as well.

So have U.S. investors stopped buying BTC, or is the discount exaggerated? By that point, Bitcoin had already closed at $64,491 on August 17, up from a 90-day low of $62,843, and climbed to $78,317 by August 21.

"Paper hands at ETFs and institutions sold the bottom," Ki Young Ju tweeted on August 25. An earlier negative streak, from January 16 to February 24, 2026, ended similarly, with the premium lagging behind price movements. The same pattern shows up among holders selling at a loss.

ETF outflows, the Coinbase discount, and Bitcoin's correlation with stocks all point to the same American investor. According to SoSoValue data, ETF outflows reached $430.2 million on November 5 and $411.9 million on November 6. In total, ETF net assets dropped from $109.3 billion on October 21 to $95.9 billion on November 6, the lowest level in the past month.

On the bright side, the Fidelity Wise Origin Bitcoin Fund ( CBOE:FBTC ) was the only fund to receive inflows on November 6, adding $42.8 million following significant outflows. However, this single inflow did little to counterbalance the widespread selling across the group.

On November 6, Glassnode put Bitcoin's 30-session correlation with the S&P 500 at 0.80. A correlation of 1 means two assets move together perfectly, so Bitcoin behaves much like a stock. When stock investors reduce their risk, they often sell Bitcoin as well. The VIX, which measures expected stock market volatility, surged to 28.18 on November 5, its highest level in 90 days.

A recovery will require U.S. investors to return through the same channels they exited. ETF flows can change quickly, as the $528.4 million inflow on October 21 showed. Investor sentiment has turned fearful following the Fear and Greed Index drop in October, but fear alone has not yet brought buyers back, and long-term holders selling into weakness continue to add supply.

While U.S. investors are still participating in the market, they appear to be net sellers for now. We believe the 61-day discount on Coinbase reflects this hesitation rather than a complete retreat from Bitcoin.

Even so, the discount alone doesn't mark a floor, since the premium has turned positive only after Bitcoin rebounded. Two signals could change that view. The first is a full week of net ETF inflows, with the Coinbase gap turning positive in the same week. The second is a daily close above the 20-day average of $79,641, then above the 50-day average of $81,974, near where recent buyers break even.

extraction.body: The ECX crypto fork gives eligible Bitcoin holders equal coin balances on eCash, a separate network whose coins require safe separation before use. Paul Sztorc’s LayerTwo Labs launched the eCash Bitcoin fork on October 29, giving holders who controlled their BTC ▼ $75,828.00 private keys at block 973,728 an equal balance of the new network’s native ECX. The ECX crypto allocation copies coin balances, not Bitcoin’s dollar value. The immediate task for eligible holders is separating the coins safely. Native ECX runs on the eCash network, while wrapped ECX, or wECX, trades on Solana. Access also depends on custody: people who held BTC on an exchange must wait for that exchange’s distribution policy. The fork began with Bitcoin’s ledger at block 973,728. Holders controlling the corresponding private keys received the same number of coins on eCash, according to LayerTwo Labs’ account of the allocation. The October 29 launch and holder-access details were examined by Cointelegraph on November 7. The allocation gives eligible holders a separate asset to access; selling it requires a compatible market and successful coin separation. ECX is the native asset of eCash, a separate hard fork developed from Bitcoin’s code. It is used on the new network rather than issued as a token on Bitcoin itself. The project’s proposed use extends beyond transferring the mainchain coin. Its Drivechain design gives developers room to build sidechains for payments, privacy, digital assets and prediction markets, with different transaction rules. Sztorc, the founder of LayerTwo Labs, is the driving force behind the Bitcoin Drivechain proposals BIP300 and BIP301. He spent more than a decade advocating for Drivechains before launching eCash. He describes Bitcoin’s conservative development approach as an obstacle to greater network use. The fork gives his team a separate network on which to pursue applications and sidechains instead of waiting for Bitcoin to adopt those changes. The project describes eCash as activating BIP300 and BIP301, allowing competing sidechains to operate under their own rules while keeping the base layer small. Bitcoin continues separately under its own protocol. Two further projects are planned: Photon, described as quantum-resistant, and CoinShift, a decentralized exchange. They remain additions to come rather than part of the initial five-sidechain launch. Sztorc identifies paying customers and transaction-fee revenue as the main first-year measures of success. That puts the commercial test on applications people choose to use and pay for, rather than the number of Bitcoin holders receiving copied balances. LayerTwo Labs says early ECX trading ranged between $40 and $50. That is the company’s description of early activity, not a current November 7 quote or a verified all-time high. Eligible self-custody holders need an eCash-compatible wallet and the project’s coin-separation process. The website links to wallet downloads, a coin-splitting section, a dashboard and a block explorer. Those published instructions matter because eCash and Bitcoin share transaction history. LayerTwo Labs says replay controls are built into the protocol, but still instructs holders to separate ECX before spending the corresponding BTC. An unprotected transaction on one network can be replayed on the other. LayerTwo Labs warns: “Never move your BTC first,” explaining that an ordinary, unprotected Bitcoin spend can also be replayed on eCash. The company’s operational advice is to move ECX first. Holders should follow its published wallet and splitting procedure rather than improvise transaction steps. People who kept BTC on a centralized exchange depend on that custodian’s fork policy. Control of a Bitcoin account balance at an exchange is different from personally controlling the private keys used for the allocation. Exchange customers should check the platform’s own support and distribution announcements. Forks can also create tax implications depending on the holder’s country, making local tax treatment another consideration before accessing or selling ECX. Critics of the Drivechain model argue that miners could coordinate to steal funds held on sidechains. That concern centers on the security of funds using those sidechains, rather than simply the existence of the copied mainchain balance. Sztorc rejects the criticism. He argues that miners would jeopardize their own businesses by pursuing a short-term theft, presenting their economic incentives as a defense of the design. Holders face a contested security model, not a settled guarantee. A separate Solana asset named eCash, also using ECX, has a PumpSwap pair created on October 10—less than 30 days before November 7. DEX Screener shows roughly $5,200 in liquidity for that pair. Its connection to the native fork or wrapped wECX has not been established. NeoxEX said it opened native ECX deposits, withdrawals and trading on October 29. Its announced markets were ECX/ USDT ▼ $0.9989 , ECX/ USDC ▼ $0.9995 and ECX/BTC. CoinW announced plans to distribute ECX to eligible Bitcoin holders, with deposits, withdrawals and trading to be announced later. Its distribution commitment should therefore be distinguished from an already operating trading market. Orca offers a liquidity pool for swapping USDC into wrapped ECX on Solana. This is trading in wECX rather than native ECX on the eCash network. The longer-term test remains Sztorc’s stated focus on paying customers and transaction fees. ECX’s prospects depend on whether the separate network turns its launch applications into sustained use, alongside safe access for existing holders. The allocation used Bitcoin block 973,728. LayerTwo Labs says people controlling their BTC private keys at that point received a matching number of native ECX coins. LayerTwo Labs developed eCash under founder Paul Sztorc. passages: The ECX crypto fork gives eligible Bitcoin holders equal coin balances on eCash, a separate network whose coins require safe separation before use.

Paul Sztorc’s LayerTwo Labs launched the eCash Bitcoin fork on October 29, giving holders who controlled their BTC ▼ $75,828.00 private keys at block 973,728 an equal balance of the new network’s native ECX. The ECX crypto allocation copies coin balances, not Bitcoin’s dollar value.

The immediate task for eligible holders is separating the coins safely. Native ECX runs on the eCash network, while wrapped ECX, or wECX, trades on Solana. Access also depends on custody: people who held BTC on an exchange must wait for that exchange’s distribution policy.

The fork began with Bitcoin’s ledger at block 973,728. Holders controlling the corresponding private keys received the same number of coins on eCash, according to LayerTwo Labs’ account of the allocation.

The October 29 launch and holder-access details were examined by Cointelegraph on November 7. The allocation gives eligible holders a separate asset to access; selling it requires a compatible market and successful coin separation.
ECX is the native asset of eCash, a separate hard fork developed from Bitcoin’s code. It is used on the new network rather than issued as a token on Bitcoin itself.

The project’s proposed use extends beyond transferring the mainchain coin. Its Drivechain design gives developers room to build sidechains for payments, privacy, digital assets and prediction markets, with different transaction rules.
Sztorc, the founder of LayerTwo Labs, is the driving force behind the Bitcoin Drivechain proposals BIP300 and BIP301. He spent more than a decade advocating for Drivechains before launching eCash.

He describes Bitcoin’s conservative development approach as an obstacle to greater network use. The fork gives his team a separate network on which to pursue applications and sidechains instead of waiting for Bitcoin to adopt those changes.

The project describes eCash as activating BIP300 and BIP301, allowing competing sidechains to operate under their own rules while keeping the base layer small. Bitcoin continues separately under its own protocol.
Two further projects are planned: Photon, described as quantum-resistant, and CoinShift, a decentralized exchange. They remain additions to come rather than part of the initial five-sidechain launch.

Sztorc identifies paying customers and transaction-fee revenue as the main first-year measures of success. That puts the commercial test on applications people choose to use and pay for, rather than the number of Bitcoin holders receiving copied balances.
LayerTwo Labs says early ECX trading ranged between $40 and $50. That is the company’s description of early activity, not a current November 7 quote or a verified all-time high.

Eligible self-custody holders need an eCash-compatible wallet and the project’s coin-separation process. The website links to wallet downloads, a coin-splitting section, a dashboard and a block explorer.

Those published instructions matter because eCash and Bitcoin share transaction history. LayerTwo Labs says replay controls are built into the protocol, but still instructs holders to separate ECX before spending the corresponding BTC.

An unprotected transaction on one network can be replayed on the other. LayerTwo Labs warns: “Never move your BTC first,” explaining that an ordinary, unprotected Bitcoin spend can also be replayed on eCash.
The company’s operational advice is to move ECX first. Holders should follow its published wallet and splitting procedure rather than improvise transaction steps.

People who kept BTC on a centralized exchange depend on that custodian’s fork policy. Control of a Bitcoin account balance at an exchange is different from personally controlling the private keys used for the allocation.

Exchange customers should check the platform’s own support and distribution announcements. Forks can also create tax implications depending on the holder’s country, making local tax treatment another consideration before accessing or selling ECX.

Critics of the Drivechain model argue that miners could coordinate to steal funds held on sidechains. That concern centers on the security of funds using those sidechains, rather than simply the existence of the copied mainchain balance.

Sztorc rejects the criticism. He argues that miners would jeopardize their own businesses by pursuing a short-term theft, presenting their economic incentives as a defense of the design. Holders face a contested security model, not a settled guarantee.

A separate Solana asset named eCash, also using ECX, has a PumpSwap pair created on October 10—less than 30 days before November 7. DEX Screener shows roughly $5,200 in liquidity for that pair. Its connection to the native fork or wrapped wECX has not been established.
NeoxEX said it opened native ECX deposits, withdrawals and trading on October 29. Its announced markets were ECX/ USDT ▼ $0.9989 , ECX/ USDC ▼ $0.9995 and ECX/BTC.

CoinW announced plans to distribute ECX to eligible Bitcoin holders, with deposits, withdrawals and trading to be announced later. Its distribution commitment should therefore be distinguished from an already operating trading market.
Orca offers a liquidity pool for swapping USDC into wrapped ECX on Solana. This is trading in wECX rather than native ECX on the eCash network.

The longer-term test remains Sztorc’s stated focus on paying customers and transaction fees. ECX’s prospects depend on whether the separate network turns its launch applications into sustained use, alongside safe access for existing holders.

facts.text: ECX crypto is the coin planned for a 2026 Bitcoin hard fork at 1:1.
This new eCash project is separate from eCash (XEC), the older cryptocurrency associated with the Bitcoin Cash lineage.
CoinCodex tracks 40,000+ cryptocurrencies on 400+ exchanges, offering live prices, price predictions, and financial tools for crypto, stocks, and forex traders.
Unlike a standard crypto airdrop that sends tokens to selected addresses, a fork requires verification of the underlying Bitcoin balance at the snapshot.
A ledger record captures Bitcoin's balances at the selected fork point.
The fork itself wouldn't subtract BTC from those balances.
Accessing a forked asset can expose the keys protecting your original Bitcoin.

extraction.body: A new Washington Post survey finds that Americans are increasingly worried about the possible fallout if the AI boom goes bust. The report was published on November 7. The concern reflects a broader shift in public sentiment. For much of the past year, AI was seen as a major growth story, with companies investing heavily in data centers, chips, and AI models. Now, investors and consumers are asking harder questions about whether that spending will pay off. The issue is especially important because AI companies are spending enormous amounts on infrastructure. Data centers require expensive chips, power, cooling, land, and networking equipment. Recent market movements have added to the pressure. Technology stocks fell sharply at the end of October as investors questioned whether massive AI investments would generate returns quickly enough. The concern is not that AI is useless. Instead, it is that the gap between AI capability and measurable business value may still be too wide for some companies. For businesses, the report is a reminder to evaluate AI vendors carefully. Companies should consider pricing stability, service reliability, data security , and the vendor’s financial health before committing to major AI projects. For employees, the AI boom may affect hiring, team structures, and job security. Companies may reduce some roles while investing more heavily in AI-related positions. The survey suggests that public trust in AI may depend not only on what the technology can do, but also on whether people believe it is being built responsibly. passages: Core Scientific ( NASDAQ:CORZ ) reported third-quarter results on November 5, 2026.

On the earnings call, CEO Adam Sullivan set a date for leaving the Bitcoin (CRYPTO:BTC) business: "We expect to complete our exit from Bitcoin mining by year-end." CFO Jim Nygaard said the company should enter 2027 as a pure-play colocation provider, which means it will only rent data center space and power to AI customers.
Every megawatt billed at Core Scientific is rented by CoreWeave ( NASDAQ:CRWV ).
Core Scientific says the billing capacity equals more than $700 million of annualized colocation revenue.
The revenue mix shows how far the shift has already gone.
Colocation brought in $215.4 million of total revenue of $232.9 million.
That works out to about 92%, up from 83.2% in the second quarter and 18.4% a year earlier.
Self-mining revenue fell to $12.3 million from $57.4 million.
Mining income rises and falls with bitcoin's price and with network difficulty, which measures how hard it is to earn new coins.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
Core Scientific carries about $4.3 billion of long-term debt, so delivery delays would hit shareholders first.
If Pecos misses that date, Core Scientific would likely remain dependent on one tenant longer, weakening the case for diversification.

extraction.body: These companies have promising prospects. They would be even more attractive on the dip. Artificial intelligence (AI) isn't just a fad. The technology is reshaping the world, and many corporations are helping power this revolution. However, investors chasing life-changing returns have bid up shares of many AI companies, some of which, despite having highly promising prospects, have become too expensive. In fact, the entire market is arguably overvalued, at least as measured by metrics such as the S&P 500 Shiller CAPE ratio, which is near its highest levels since before the dot-com bubble burst. We may eventually experience a bear market as a result, and if we do, there are three stocks I can't wait to buy on the dip: Space Exploration Technologies ( SPCX +8.62% ) , Tesla ( TSLA +4.23% ) , and CoreWeave ( CRWV +6.28% ) . Here is why. Space Exploration Technologies is best known for revolutionizing space travel . The company helped pioneer reusable rocket technology, thereby significantly reducing launch costs. However, SpaceX's AI business, which it recently renamed Super Intelligence (SI), has arguably been more impressive than its space business since it went public in June. In the third quarter, SpaceX's revenue increased by 161% year over year to $14.6 billion. Space revenue grew 6% year over year to $1.8 billion, while SI revenue soared 830% year over year to $7.6 billion. The company's connectivity revenue was $5.2 billion, up 69.5% year over year. So, SI now accounts for more than half of the company's revenue and is growing much faster than other business segments. It is also profitable. SI operating income for the period was $431 million, significantly better than the operating loss of $1.7 billion reported in the year-ago period. SpaceX's space business isn't profitable, though its connectivity business is. But SI could remain the main growth driver, as SpaceX is experiencing outstanding demand for AI compute capacity. However, the stock remains fairly expensive -- it is trading at 50.8x forward earnings, and there is significant uncertainty ahead, including with the company's development of its next-gen rocket , Starship, which could support many of its AI-related ambitions. The business looks promising, but it is too risky at current levels. If the stock falls at least 25%, I'd buy without a second thought. CoreWeave, a neocloud company, is also seeing booming demand for its services. Second-quarter revenue grew 112.5% year over year to $2.6 billion, while its revenue backlog was $104 billion, up 245.5% compared to the year-ago period. The problem is that CoreWeave is spending significant sums to keep purchasing AI infrastructure. The company's debt has ballooned as a result, while operating and net losses are worsening year over year. In the second quarter, CoreWeave posted an operating loss of $49 million, down from the operating income of $19 million reported in the year-ago period. Its net loss per share widened to $1.14, compared with $0.60 per share in the prior-year quarter. CoreWeave has raised more than $30 billion this year. Perhaps that won't be a problem for the company as long as AI spending continues to grow unabated. But if it doesn't, the company could be in trouble. My view is that CoreWeave is an attractive AI stock , but the mounting debt and customer concentration -- a single customer accounted for 67% of its revenue in 2025 -- leave little room for error at current levels. Investors with an appetite for risk may still consider initiating a small position in the company, but I'd feel even more comfortable doing so if the stock loses 15% to 20%. Tesla is a different kind of AI company. It doesn't offer AI compute capacity like CoreWeave and SpaceX, but the technology has become central to its future. Tesla has several AI-heavy projects, including its robotaxi and humanoid robot ambitions. AI helps the company train its self-driving vehicles, and it could also allow Tesla to improve its Optimus robots. There might be a large market in both cases. Provided Optimus robots are as advanced as Tesla wants them to be, they could be in high demand in factories and warehouses and eventually make their way into the home. Meanwhile, Tesla's robotaxi business could generate significant profits at scale. However, there is plenty of uncertainty. Regulators will have their say in both markets, and the public may not adopt these technologies to the extent Tesla hopes. Could the business still perform well over the long run? Absolutely, but to be as sure as possible that I'd earn juicy returns, I'd like to buy the stock at a much lower price -- Tesla is currently trading at 163.2x forward earnings. At those prices, the $1,000 invested now could be worth approximately $1,977, $2,636, or $3,295, depending on how much new demand enters the market. So, what would it take for your $1,000 investment from November 2026 to double or even triple by 2030?

Will Bitcoin hit $100,000 again? Its last monthly close above that mark came in October 2025, at around $109,555. If Bitcoin returns to that level, your $1,000 could grow to about $1,318. To roughly double your investment, Bitcoin would need to reach $150,000, a 97.7% increase from the current price that would carry it well past its previous all-time high.
A breakdown of what 0.1 Bitcoin could be worth by 2030 applies the same math to a larger holding.

Bitcoin’s market cap is calculated by multiplying the price of one coin by the total number of coins in circulation. Bitcoin’s market cap is about $1.53 trillion, so each target price above requires far more money to flow into the network.

As new coins are continuously mined, known as supply dilution, the required market cap for these price levels increases each year. Bitcoin’s circulating supply has reached 20,105,365 BTC, up from 20,103,596 BTC on October 26, and it keeps growing toward the 21,000,000 cap. So if Bitcoin reaches $150,000, its market value would need to hit $3.02 trillion based on the current supply and $3.15 trillion once the full cap is reached.

The supply in 2030 is projected to be higher, but it will never surpass 21,000,000 BTC. To match the previous all-time high, the market would need about $2.53 trillion at the current supply level. At $250,000, Bitcoin would need a $5.03 trillion market cap, about double what a new all-time high requires.

Spot Bitcoin ETFs are investment funds that hold Bitcoin directly, and they drove the previous price surge. However, the funds posted a $430.2 million outflow on November 5, after a $74.6 million inflow the day before.

Cumulative net inflows, which represent total new money since the ETFs launched, fell from $57.96 billion on October 21 to $56.11 billion on November 5, according to SoSoValue. Total assets in the funds also fell from $109.31 billion to $96.65 billion over the same period.

Historically, Bitcoin has rallied after U.S. midterm elections . According to Binance Research, Bitcoin fell 56% in 2014, 73% in 2018, and 64% in 2022, then rose an average of 54% in the year after each vote. Bitcoin is down 13.4% so far in 2026, and while history suggests potential for recovery, it will depend on whether new buyers come into the market.

Bitcoin undergoes a “halving” approximately every four years, which cuts the rewards miners receive for creating new coins. The next halving is anticipated in 2028. After the April 2024 halving, Bitcoin rose from around $60,762 to $96,436 by November 2024, then peaked approximately 18 months after the halving. If that cycle repeats, the next peak could arrive in late 2029 or 2030, right around the horizon for money invested in November 2026.

Analyst Beth Kindig has noted the recent strengthening of the U.S. dollar and rising yields, linking this trend to Bitcoin’s decline from its peak. If the dollar continues to appreciate and ETF investments remain low, Bitcoin may revisit its 2026 lows.

Bitcoin has a good chance of trading above $100,000 again by 2030 and a fair chance of reaching $150,000, where $1,000 would be worth about $1,977, close to double. Prices of $250,000 and $500,000 look unlikely, because they need a market value above $5 trillion while ETF buyers are still pulling money out.

Bitcoin first has to hold its 200-day moving average of $73,197, then recover its 50-day average of $82,003 and its September high near $87,397, clear $100,000, and close a month above $126,080. A monthly close below the June low of $58,566 could put $150,000 out of reach this cycle. For any Bitcoin price prediction for 2030 that doubles $1,000, the first signal is cumulative ETF inflows climbing back above $57.96 billion.

Will Bitcoin hit $100,000 again? Its last monthly close above that mark came in October 2025, at around $109,555. If Bitcoin returns to that level, your $1,000 could grow to about $1,318. To roughly double your investment, Bitcoin would need to reach $150,000, a 97.7% increase from the current price that would carry it well past its previous all-time high.
A breakdown of what 0.1 Bitcoin could be worth by 2030 applies the same math to a larger holding.

Bitcoin’s market cap is calculated by multiplying the price of one coin by the total number of coins in circulation. Bitcoin’s market cap is about $1.53 trillion, so each target price above requires far more money to flow into the network.

As new coins are continuously mined, known as supply dilution, the required market cap for these price levels increases each year. Bitcoin’s circulating supply has reached 20,105,365 BTC, up from 20,103,596 BTC on October 26, and it keeps growing toward the 21,000,000 cap. So if Bitcoin reaches $150,000, its market value would need to hit $3.02 trillion based on the current supply and $3.15 trillion once the full cap is reached.

The supply in 2030 is projected to be higher, but it will never surpass 21,000,000 BTC. To match the previous all-time high, the market would need about $2.53 trillion at the current supply level. At $250,000, Bitcoin would need a $5.03 trillion market cap, about double what a new all-time high requires.

Spot Bitcoin ETFs are investment funds that hold Bitcoin directly, and they drove the previous price surge. However, the funds posted a $430.2 million outflow on November 5, after a $74.6 million inflow the day before.

Cumulative net inflows, which represent total new money since the ETFs launched, fell from $57.96 billion on October 21 to $56.11 billion on November 5, according to SoSoValue. Total assets in the funds also fell from $109.31 billion to $96.65 billion over the same period.

Historically, Bitcoin has rallied after U.S. midterm elections . According to Binance Research, Bitcoin fell 56% in 2014, 73% in 2018, and 64% in 2022, then rose an average of 54% in the year after each vote. Bitcoin is down 13.4% so far in 2026, and while history suggests potential for recovery, it will depend on whether new buyers come into the market.

Bitcoin undergoes a “halving” approximately every four years, which cuts the rewards miners receive for creating new coins. The next halving is anticipated in 2028. After the April 2024 halving, Bitcoin rose from around $60,762 to $96,436 by November 2024, then peaked approximately 18 months after the halving. If that cycle repeats, the next peak could arrive in late 2029 or 2030, right around the horizon for money invested in November 2026.

Analyst Beth Kindig has noted the recent strengthening of the U.S. dollar and rising yields, linking this trend to Bitcoin’s decline from its peak. If the dollar continues to appreciate and ETF investments remain low, Bitcoin may revisit its 2026 lows.

Bitcoin has a good chance of trading above $100,000 again by 2030 and a fair chance of reaching $150,000, where $1,000 would be worth about $1,977, close to double. Prices of $250,000 and $500,000 look unlikely, because they need a market value above $5 trillion while ETF buyers are still pulling money out.

A monthly close below the June low of $58,566 could put $150,000 out of reach this cycle. Put your iPad to good use with apps for journaling, discovering art and much more. Our favorite apps are elegant and well-designed, taking advantage of the entire iPad display.

extraction.body: Put your iPad to good use with apps for journaling, discovering art and much more. Your iPad should make every day easier. Whether you want to build new habits or improve your routines, we've rounded up apps that put the best iPads to work in your daily life. We found these by digging a bit deeper. These aren't first-party Apple apps or subscription-only Adobe staples. It's free to get started with each, though most charge for extra features, which we've noted where applicable. Our favorite apps are elegant and well-designed, taking advantage of the entire iPad display. They also keep AI to a bare minimum. There may be machine learning to help with search and transcriptions, but you won't find fake images or bogus text generators here. If you're a voracious consumer of media, you need Sofa to help keep track of it all. Start with books, TV shows and movies, then add whatever other categories you'd like. Sofa has a clean interface that grabs title images and info to give you an overview of everything you watch (or read). Sofa's tracking feature is especially useful for remembering which episodes you've seen. Mark them off as you watch them and add notes if you like, or rely on the included summaries. Sofa tracks two different series at once for free, while paid subscribers can track unlimited titles. Sofa's free tier offers all its best features without advertisements or pop-ups begging for more. If you want to fine-tune your media tracking with custom ratings that you create and smart lists that populate based on your filters, Sofa offers a subscription for $5.99 per month, $49.99 per year or $249.99 for a lifetime membership. Unless you're a professional TV critic, you'll likely be fine with the free features. Instead of Apple Notes or Google Keep, try Bear , an app for capturing thoughts. Bear has become a productivity favorite by keeping its interface deceptively simple; it's a large notepad app without a glut of buttons and menus. While it's powerful, you don't have to use advanced features you don't need. Bear is built around smooth Markdown styling and supports tags to organize your thoughts. For example, if you find yourself often complaining about your job, tag that post with #job . You can add links, tags or even to-do tasks that are easily searchable. If that sounds complicated, ignore what you don't need and you're left with an elegant, attractive note-taking and journaling app. Bear has a reasonably-priced subscription tier ($3/month or $30/year) that offers a few extra features if you're hardcore about your notes. With it, you can sync your Bear notes between devices, as well as publish your notes using HTML or ePub to use the app as a blogging tool. After a few minutes with Flipboard , you'll wonder why it isn't preloaded on every iPad. This decentralized social experience transforms the touchscreen into a magazine with a clean layout and large images. If you read a lot of news, Flipboard is the best way to stay current. The app starts by having you select from an endless list of topics to find stories. These can start as general as sports, music or science. Or by dialing down, you might find "UEFA Champions League," "blues music" or "sustainable design." If any sources arise that you don't want to see, block them. In general, the selection is great; you can follow individual authors and sites the same way you follow topics. The best part about Flipboard is that it's totally free: it doesn't make you cough up a fee for the best content, and you can sometimes find stories that are normally trapped behind a paywall. HappySpoon is an (artificially) intelligent meal planner that helps you create a menu for the week ahead following whatever ideas or guidelines you set. The app uses AI to understand plain-language requests that you make, like "I need to use up all my chicken breast, so make a bunch of different chicken recipes." Once you've created your menu, it even generates a handy shopping list sorted by grocery store aisle. I asked the app to generate "breakfasts that are simple and on-repeat, like a big batch of muffins or oatmeal to eat every day" and it did exactly that. It also understood the rule "no lunches" and left that spot blank on my weekly menu. HappySpoon automatically resizes your portions and recipes to match your eaters. You can specify adult-sized or kid-sized appetites, and it will conform: the grocery list populates with the right amounts. You don't need to use HappySpoon's AI features; in fact, they're only free for two weeks. That's enough time to get started and use the AI for help generating a variety of menus. There are plenty of other AI tools that can create recipes, but if you want to stick with HappySpoon, the fee is $5.99 per month or $49.99 per year. I found the AI tools useful at first, but after a couple of weeks, the extra AI benefits didn't seem necessary. Whatever you need to organize, MindNode is a perfect starting point. Whether it's a meeting agenda, a workout plan or your life's goals, MindNode offers a simple canvas to connect and organize thoughts. You'll find features to enhance, stylize and reorganize your finished maps. Start with the big idea in the center and then branch out. A map can grow large the more you dig in, but MindNode makes it easy to keep your idea maps looking neat. You also have the option to view your maps as a text outline instead. If this sort of mental organization appeals to you, the premium subscription may offer enough bonus features to make it worth the asking $2.99 per month or $24.99 per year. With the subscription, you get more editing tools, the ability to add photos and emoji to your nodes and some professional-strength features for teams working together. It also unlocks real-time collaboration with others so you see edits and additions as they happen. You can set each node as a task with a reminder and checklist. And Apple Intelligence will enhance the experience by offering new ideas, summarizing what it sees and similar. The AI extras aren't necessary, but are available with the premium plan. Journey is a place to store your memories, including journal entries, calendar appointments , major dates, photos, multimedia and maps of the places you've been. The more you use Journey, the more it rewards your dedication, with features that track your habits later on. The available templates are Journey's secret weapon. If you're planning a trip, for example, the travel planner template includes fields for details like your hotel address, flight information, car rental details and even a budget planner that tracks your anticipated versus actual spending. Templates include tons of other categories, from personal goal trackers to a 30-60-90 day plan for starting a new career. Once you've built a journaling habit, you're able to track your progress through Journey's graphs and statistics. If you tag each journal entry with a mood, you'll see how your feelings ebbed and flowed throughout your journaling experience. By paying $6.99 per month or $49.99 per year (or $199 for the app's lifetime), you get premium features that could be helpful if you share a journal with someone else. There's also a premium AI feature included, though thankfully it doesn't offer to write journal entries for you. Instead, you can ask "how many entries did I write last month?" or tell it to "summarize my summer vacation from 2026." Libby is your local library in app form , which should be enough to earn an immediate download. Did you know you can borrow ebooks from your library? Just register your library card with Libby — go get one if you don't have one! — and you're ready to download the glut of digital content you might not have even known your library offered. Day One will record an unlimited number of journal entries without paying a dime, but if you want to add unlimited photos and videos, or audio recordings, you'll need to pay a subscription fee. For $49.99/year you get all that, plus interesting integration with IFTTT (If This Then That) and other markup tools. Habitify can help you build habits without being intrusive or making you do so much work that the app becomes its own "habit" to maintain. You design a habit or goal, then Habitify monitors your progress in the background as much as it can. It's the rare app that you barely need to use to get value from. You tell Habitify what you want to do and on which days you'll repeat the habit, then give it a specific goal. Habitify integrates neatly with Siri, so you often won't need to open the app to log your habit since Siri will. Siri can even update you on your progress — just ask how you're doing with your goals and Habitify will feed Siri the answer. There is a paid option for $49.99 per year, which is useful if fitness is your goal since Apple Health and Google Health integrations sit behind that paywall. You can connect Habitify to your Apple Watch or Fitbit so it knows you kept up your routine. It works with Apple Health and Google Health to gather data, with your permission. The paid option can also monitor your screen time if limits are part of your habit goals. DailyArt is for art world enthusiasts who want to go beyond the most prolific canvases and dive deeper into the lives of the artists who created them. One recent offering was a gorgeous Autumn Landscape created in 1899 by the pseudonymous Hishida Shunsō. In addition to the image, the app offers a brief history of the work and artist, with an explanation of the style it exemplifies. You can select the artist name or other links to see more artwork, or wait until tomorrow to see what DailyArt serves up next.
