extraction.body: Democrats’ historic victory in this week’s midterm elections could also have a dramatic effect on the tech industry. In dozens of local ballot measures, voters rejected data centers . And even when they weren’t voting on the issue directly, they were electing politicians — like Texas’ new governor-elect Gina Hinojosa — who campaigned on the promise of restricting data centers. On the latest episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast , Kirsten Korosec, Sean O’Kane, and I discussed what the midterms mean for the tech industry. Sean kicked it off by noting that Elon Musk “seems to have basically nothing out of donating half a billion dollars” to Republicans, while his companies are now headquartered “in a state that has, remarkably, turned about as blue as it could possibly turn.” And Kirsten said that while data centers probably weren’t the main cause of the “blue wave,” they’ve become an “an increasingly grassroots issue, in part because of how hyperscalers and companies have gone about” getting their projects approved. And now, “we’re already seeing companies like OpenAI all of a sudden go, ‘Actually, we can change our policies.’” Keep reading for a preview of our conversation , edited for length and clarity. Sean O’Kane: First off, let’s talk about the fact that one of the biggest data center builders was also the largest donor to the Republican Party. Elon Musk seems to have gotten basically nothing out of donating half a billion dollars — maybe even more, by the time we see the final count — and in fact is now sitting there with all of his businesses in a state that has, remarkably, turned about as blue as it could possibly turn for the first time in a very long time, if ever. That, I think, is the biggest thing hanging above a lot of this discussion. But, there were also a bunch of ballot measures up around the country that would have paved the way for data centers to get built faster. Almost all of them got shot down, or voted against. [Actually, many of the ballot measures would have imposed restrictions or moratoriums on data centers, and almost all of those measures passed.] With [Democrats] in power, there is a consensus view, at least in the tech world, that this is going to mean we have a lot of roadblocks ahead for data centers, especially in places like Texas, where [you have] folks like the governor-elect [Gina] Hinojosa, who has spoken pretty openly about this being a campaign promise and something that she wants to focus on once she takes power, now that she’s beaten Greg Abbott. It’s the thing that I think the tech world is maybe a little too focused on. I’m curious what you guys think about that. Anthony Ha: I don’t necessarily think that they’re too focused on it, but I understand why it would feel a little bit disproportionate — the data center ballot measures, certainly there were a number of them, but it wasn’t something that was on the ballot everywhere. And in different races, the dynamic might have been a bit different, but there was this undercurrent and sense that it seems to be an issue that reaches across the country, that is bipartisan in a lot of ways, but that the Democrats seem to have been more effective at harnessing that energy. And of course, there’s all kinds of reasons why the Democrats did so well on Tuesday, but it does seem like anti-AI and especially anti-data center sentiment was a big part of it. That seems like a pretty potent political force. The next two years, [and] potentially beyond that, are going to be more difficult for tech companies in general, and hyperscalers, data center companies in particular. I also imagine that they have to be a little bit worried about: Is this going to continue to be an issue, not just with the people who got elected this year, but potentially in 2028 and beyond? Kirsten Korosec: Absolutely. I don’t think that the data center issue is what brought everyone to the polls and led to the quote-unquote “blue wave.” However, I will say that data centers have been an increasingly grassroots issue, in part because of how hyperscalers and companies have gone about getting these data centers [approved] — very secretive, oftentimes requiring NDAs of a elected officials or appointed officials, not sharing information about the scale of a project in very environmentally sensitive areas, including in the Southwest, where there’s very much a water scarcity issue. So I think that a lot of folks — Republicans, independents, and Democrats — all saw this as wrong. They were motivated by it, but I don’t think it was a singular issue. Now, here’s the interesting thing. There was a lot of waving of hands about how [AI companies] can’t possibly operate under any other circumstances. And we’re already seeing companies like OpenAI all of a sudden go, “Actually, we can change our policies.” They just released what they call a compute campus policy blueprint . And guess what? They’re not going to require NDAs anymore. They’re going to share their plans and supposedly operate in less secrecy. I think what this shows is that when you put up either a regulatory certainty in the marketplace, or at least signals of going in that direction, then corporations will respond. If you don’t do that, they will not necessarily do the thing that we hope that they will do. Anthony: One thing I want to emphasize is that they’re calling it this [their] “compute campus policy.” And part of what that’s doing, beyond laying out these policy changes, is also an attempt to rebrand data centers, because they have become such a toxic phrase. So they’re not data centers anymore, they are compute campuses, and I’m curious, whether either of you think that’ll take. Sean: I mean, this is ridiculous. Come on. It’s not going to change anything. It’s going to cause them more effort. For a company that likes to say that it’s no longer focused on side quests, OpenAI still loves to go in different directions a lot. And this is just the latest kind of thing where it’s just like: Why are you spending time on this at all? It doesn’t really seem like it’s going to move the needle. Kirsten: I have a great idea for OpenAI. Because in the spirit of making threatening things seem cute, they should 100% create a compute campuses avatar, [a] cutesy thing, and then just present that instead of a power-, energy-sucking, water-sucking data center. Anthony: And if these are just lovely compute campuses, they should just build their own offices there or work next door, see how that works out for them. Something else that I’m wondering about is, to what extent the election is maybe the second part of a one-two punch. [We’ve just seen] a big shift in how Wall Street is reacting to a lot of these hyperscalers and AI companies and this sense that [investors] are not excited about the idea that they should be spending all this money building new data centers, spending all this money on compute. And so there’s a financial incentive not to build all these data centers. I’m very curious how that’s going to play out. [From a regulatory standpoint,] it’s probably going to be harder to build data centers. Wall Street is probably not going to reward you for building data centers. But at the same time, to get to the scale that they want to get to, they are probably going to need to build data centers somewhere. While the debate over the future of artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure spending continues to rage on Wall Street, many corporations aren't just saying they will spend more on AI; they are backing up their words with action. So far this earnings season, we have seen that many leaders in the field are still pouring fortunes into hopes of capitalizing on what they see as a transformative opportunity. This provides strong evidence that the ongoing AI revolution isn't over yet, and there is still time to invest in stocks that could ride this tailwind over the long run. Here are four great examples to consider: Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA), Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT), Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ:AMD), and Broadcom (NASDAQ:AVGO). Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » Nvidia's indispensable role in the industry has made it one of the biggest winners of the AI revolution so far. In my view, that's likely to remain the case over the long run. Despite increased competition in the GPU ( graphics processing unit ) market, the company has maintained a runaway lead. This has a lot to do with the company's wide moat, thanks to its CUDA ecosystem, which creates high switching costs. Demand for GPUs may not be quite as impressive moving forward as it has been in recent years, but Nvidia has expanded beyond its core market. The company's existing relationships with many corporations that continue to rely on its GPUs can enable it to offer these clients other hardware and services that complement -- and work best with -- its GPUs for training, deploying, and running AI models. That puts Nvidia in a good position to ride the AI tailwind. Microsoft is proving the doubters wrong. Some investors feared that AI would make its services obsolete, since the technology has reduced software development costs. But Microsoft has adapted. Its cloud business is booming, in part thanks to its library of AI services. It has also integrated AI across its productivity suite. Meanwhile, the company boasts a massive and rapidly growing cloud backlog. These are all signs that Microsoft may continue cashing in on AI, at least over the next few years. And beyond that, the company's ability to deliver consistent revenue and earnings, strong cash position, and innovative capabilities grant it the opportunity to tap into an AI market that could continue to expand over the long run. Advanced Micro Devices has also benefited from an increased demand for GPUs, although it has played second fiddle to Nvidia in that market. However, the company is now seeing soaring demand for CPUs (central processing units). Recent financial results have been excellent, particularly for the company's data center segment. The advent of AI agents -- which run on CPUs -- could be a powerful long-term tailwind. In fact, it has even surprised management. AMD has increased its 2030 total addressable opportunity guidance several times over the past year. The company could face more competition, but it also benefits from a competitive edge. It boasts significant technological expertise in this industry -- where it has been a leader for decades -- deep relationships with corporations, and high switching costs. All good reasons why AMD's outlook appears attractive. Broadcom could become increasingly important in the AI industry. The company designs custom AI chips, which are seeing rising demand as corporations seek to diversify away from Nvidia by buying custom chips that aren't as versatile but are often cheaper and much more power-efficient than GPUs. That doesn't mean the GPU market will shrink substantially, but as AI infrastructure scales, an increasingly large share could shift toward custom AI chips, and Broadcom will cash in on this. The company is a leader in this niche and has relationships with major AI companies, including Meta Platforms (NASDAQ:META), Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOG) (NASDAQ:GOOGL), and Anthropic, the corporation behind Claude, which is expected to go public soon. Broadcom's AI semiconductor business has lower margins than its infrastructure software segment, but over the long run, the lower gross margins will be worth it, as Broadcom's total revenue and earnings growth maintain a solid pace thanks to the continued rise in AI infrastructure spending. The stock could beat the market along the way. While the debate over the future of artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure spending continues to rage on Wall Street, many corporations aren't just saying they will spend more on AI; they are backing up their words with action. So far this earnings season, we have seen that many leaders in the field are still pouring fortunes into hopes of capitalizing on what they see as a transformative opportunity. This provides strong evidence that the ongoing AI revolution isn't over yet, and there is still time to invest in stocks that could ride this tailwind over the long run. Here are four great examples to consider: Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA), Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT), Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ:AMD), and Broadcom (NASDAQ:AVGO).

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Nvidia's indispensable role in the industry has made it one of the biggest winners of the AI revolution so far. In my view, that's likely to remain the case over the long run. Despite increased competition in the GPU ( graphics processing unit ) market, the company has maintained a runaway lead.

This has a lot to do with the company's wide moat, thanks to its CUDA ecosystem, which creates high switching costs. Demand for GPUs may not be quite as impressive moving forward as it has been in recent years, but Nvidia has expanded beyond its core market.

The company's existing relationships with many corporations that continue to rely on its GPUs can enable it to offer these clients other hardware and services that complement -- and work best with -- its GPUs for training, deploying, and running AI models. That puts Nvidia in a good position to ride the AI tailwind.

Microsoft is proving the doubters wrong. Some investors feared that AI would make its services obsolete, since the technology has reduced software development costs. But Microsoft has adapted. Its cloud business is booming, in part thanks to its library of AI services. It has also integrated AI across its productivity suite.

Meanwhile, the company boasts a massive and rapidly growing cloud backlog. These are all signs that Microsoft may continue cashing in on AI, at least over the next few years. And beyond that, the company's ability to deliver consistent revenue and earnings, strong cash position, and innovative capabilities grant it the opportunity to tap into an AI market that could continue to expand over the long run.

Advanced Micro Devices has also benefited from an increased demand for GPUs, although it has played second fiddle to Nvidia in that market. However, the company is now seeing soaring demand for CPUs (central processing units). Recent financial results have been excellent, particularly for the company's data center segment. The advent of AI agents -- which run on CPUs -- could be a powerful long-term tailwind.

In fact, it has even surprised management. AMD has increased its 2030 total addressable opportunity guidance several times over the past year. The company could face more competition, but it also benefits from a competitive edge. It boasts significant technological expertise in this industry -- where it has been a leader for decades -- deep relationships with corporations, and high switching costs. All good reasons why AMD's outlook appears attractive.

Broadcom could become increasingly important in the AI industry. The company designs custom AI chips, which are seeing rising demand as corporations seek to diversify away from Nvidia by buying custom chips that aren't as versatile but are often cheaper and much more power-efficient than GPUs.
That doesn't mean the GPU market will shrink substantially, but as AI infrastructure scales, an increasingly large share could shift toward custom AI chips, and Broadcom will cash in on this.

The company is a leader in this niche and has relationships with major AI companies, including Meta Platforms (NASDAQ:META), Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOG) (NASDAQ:GOOGL), and Anthropic, the corporation behind Claude, which is expected to go public soon. Broadcom's AI semiconductor business has lower margins than its infrastructure software segment, but over the long run, the lower gross margins will be worth it, as Broadcom's total revenue and earnings growth maintain a solid pace thanks to the continued rise in AI infrastructure spending. The stock could beat the market along the way.

The streak's length depends on who is measuring it. CoinGlass, which tracks its own index, recorded 38 consecutive negative days as of October 31, while Coinbase Markets reported 61 days by November 6, because each source uses distinct price data and thresholds. At just -0.13%, the gap is also small, and arbitrage desks, traders who buy on the cheaper exchange and sell on the pricier one, could quickly close it once U.S. buyers return.

This premium figure also has a crucial limitation. It only includes transactions in Coinbase's public order book, while larger trades often happen over the counter, away from public view. As a result, the discount could look the same even if American investors are quietly accumulating Bitcoin off-exchange. On-chain data has the same weakness, as our look at whales pulling Bitcoin off exchanges showed.

Past negative streaks have ended only after Bitcoin's price had already rebounded. For example, CoinGlass's record stretch lasted 97 days, from May 19 to August 24, 2026, before turning positive at 0.0052%. By that point, Bitcoin had already closed at $64,491 on August 17, up from a 90-day low of $62,843, and climbed to $78,317 by August 21.

"Paper hands at ETFs and institutions sold the bottom," Ki Young Ju tweeted on August 25. An earlier negative streak, from January 16 to February 24, 2026, ended similarly, with the premium lagging behind price movements. The same pattern shows up among holders selling at a loss.

ETF outflows, the Coinbase discount, and Bitcoin's correlation with stocks all point to the same American investor. According to SoSoValue data, ETF outflows reached $430.2 million on November 5 and $411.9 million on November 6. In total, ETF net assets dropped from $109.3 billion on October 21 to $95.9 billion on November 6, the lowest level in the past month.

On the bright side, the Fidelity Wise Origin Bitcoin Fund ( CBOE:FBTC ) was the only fund to receive inflows on November 6, adding $42.8 million following significant outflows. However, this single inflow did little to counterbalance the widespread selling across the group.

On November 6, Glassnode put Bitcoin's 30-session correlation with the S&P 500 at 0.80. A correlation of 1 means two assets move together perfectly, so Bitcoin behaves much like a stock. When stock investors reduce their risk, they often sell Bitcoin as well. The VIX, which measures expected stock market volatility, surged to 28.18 on November 5, its highest level in 90 days.

A recovery will require U.S. investors to return through the same channels they exited. ETF flows can change quickly, as the $528.4 million inflow on October 21 showed. Investor sentiment has turned fearful following the Fear and Greed Index drop in October, but fear alone has not yet brought buyers back, and long-term holders selling into weakness continue to add supply.

While U.S. investors are still participating in the market, they appear to be net sellers for now. We believe the 61-day discount on Coinbase reflects this hesitation rather than a complete retreat from Bitcoin.

Even so, the discount alone doesn't mark a floor, since the premium has turned positive only after Bitcoin rebounded. Two signals could change that view.
